metaTitle: Best Rivet Guns for Metal Work
metaDescription: Seven rivet guns compared by type: cordless, hand and pneumatic, with rivet size range, pulling force and nosepieces for sheet metal, trim and aircraft work.
expertTake: The DEWALT 20V MAX XR cordless rivet tool is our top pick for steady speed and 3/16 inch capacity on a battery you may already own. The Arrow heavy duty hand riveter kit is the value pick for occasional sheet metal work. Anyone setting more than a few dozen rivets a month by hand should skip manual tools and buy a cordless or air riveter.
introParagraphs: A rivet gun sets a blind rivet by pulling its mandrel until the rivet body swells on the far side of the work and the mandrel snaps off. It joins sheet metal, trim and panels from one side, where a bolt would need access to both.

Tool types differ in speed, force and cost. Hand riveters are cheap and portable, cordless tools save your hands, and pneumatic guns suit solid rivets. This guide compares seven tools across those groups and explains how to match rivet size and material.

products.name: DEWALT 20V MAX XR cordless rivet tool DCF403B, 3/16 inch, bare tool

specList.label: Pull force
specList.value: Up to 2,100 lbf, per the maker

products.description:
The DEWALT DCF403B is a cordless rivet tool with a brushless motor, a stated pulling force of up to 2,100 pounds and a 3/16 inch capacity. A tool free nose change and onboard nosepiece storage speed up switching between sizes.

The maker says it can set about 800 rivets per charge, a figure that depends on the rivet size and material, so expect fewer with 3/16 inch steel. It sells as a bare tool, so you need a battery and charger from the 20V MAX platform. Compared with the Milwaukee M12, the DEWALT offers a larger rivet capacity and more force. Compared with hand tools, it saves your wrist and is far faster over many rivets.

Ownership centers on the nose and mandrel debris. Empty the mandrel catcher regularly, keep the jaws clean and use the right nosepiece for the rivet. Store the tool with a partial battery charge. A practical tip for the DEWALT: set the first rivet in scrap of the same thickness to confirm the nosepiece and grip range, because a 3/16 inch steel rivet needs the full stroke and a short rivet will stall the tool.
products.bestFor: Auto body, HVAC and sheet metal workers who set many rivets.
pros: Cordless tool sets rivets up to 3/16 inch
Brushless motor with a stated 2,100 lbf pull
Tool free nose change speeds up size swaps
Uses the common 20V MAX battery platform
cons: Sold as a bare tool, so a battery is extra
Much higher cost than hand riveters

products.name: Milwaukee 2550-20 M12 rivet tool, 3/32 to 3/16 inch, bare tool

specList.label: Productivity
specList.value: 450 1/8 inch steel rivets per charge, maker figure

products.description:
The Milwaukee M12 rivet tool pulls rivets from 3/32 to 3/16 inch and runs on the compact M12 battery. The maker lists 450 rivets of 1/8 inch steel per charge, which is a useful benchmark for the tool's capacity.

The smaller platform keeps the tool light and easy to carry, which is a benefit in tight spots like HVAC ductwork and van conversions. Compared with the DEWALT 20V, the Milwaukee is smaller and lighter, but has less stated force and fewer rivets per charge. Compared with the Marson hand riveter, it is faster and less tiring, though much more expensive.

Ownership is similar to other cordless tools. Clean the nose and jaws, empty the mandrel catcher and use the correct nosepiece. Because it sells as a bare tool, you need an M12 battery and charger. For example, a van conversion with a few hundred 1/8 inch aluminum rivets is well within a single M12 battery, while a day of 3/16 inch steel rivets will need a spare pack.
products.bestFor: Installers who want a light cordless tool for tight spaces.
pros: Compact M12 size is light and easy to carry
Fits tight spaces better than larger tools
cons: Less stated force than the DEWALT

products.name: Marson HP-2 professional hand riveter, aluminum body, vinyl grips

specList.label: Fulcrum pin
specList.value: Square shoulder, cold formed, heat treated steel

products.description:
The Marson HP-2 is a professional grade hand riveter with a high strength aluminum alloy body and a square shouldered fulcrum pin of cold formed, heat treated steel. The square shoulder stops the pin from rotating, which is a common failure point on cheaper tools.

A manual tool is slower than a cordless one, but it has no battery to charge and is dependable over many years. The vinyl grips are comfortable for a moderate run of rivets. Compared with the Arrow, the Marson is better built and costs more. Compared with the DEWALT, it is a fraction of the cost but far more tiring for large jobs.

Ownership is about the jaws and nose. Clean aluminum shavings out of the head, replace worn jaws and keep the pivot lightly oiled. Use rivets matched to the nosepiece. For a metal roof or sign shop that sets perhaps twenty rivets an hour, the Marson is comfortable; beyond that, the repetitive squeeze starts to cost accuracy.
products.bestFor: Tradespeople who want a durable manual riveter for occasional use.
pros: Square shoulder pin resists rotation failures
Aluminum alloy body keeps weight down
cons: Manual effort is tiring over many rivets
Costs more than basic kit riveters

products.name: Arrow heavy duty riveter kit with 120 assorted rivets, extended nose
products.description:
The Arrow kit pairs a manual riveter with an extended nose and four nosepieces, plus 120 assorted rivets. It handles rivet diameters from 3/32 to 5/32 inch, which covers gutters, trim, signs and light sheet metal.

The extended nose reaches into tight spots, and the included rivets mean you can start immediately. Compared with the BILITOOLS, the Arrow has a long established brand and a more traditional two handed build. Compared with the Marson, it sits at a lower cost tier and is meant for lighter use.

Ownership is simple. Clean mandrel stubs from the nose, keep the nosepieces together and oil the pivot occasionally. For steel rivets, the manual effort is high, so use aluminum rivets when you can. The kit's 3/32, 1/8 and 5/32 inch rivets match its nosepieces, so a first project such as a gutter splice or a license plate bracket can be finished straight from the box.
products.bestFor: Homeowners and hobbyists who want a complete starter kit.
pros: Recognized brand at a low cost tier
cons: Manual effort is high on steel rivets

products.name: BILITOOLS 9 inch one hand pop rivet gun, 27 to 1 leverage, tool free nosepieces
products.description:
The BILITOOLS is a 9 inch one handed riveter with a stated 27 to 1 leverage ratio that multiplies hand force. Knurled one piece nosepieces change by hand without a wrench, and one stays installed while the others are stored.

A one hand design is helpful when you need the other hand to hold the work, but the shorter handle limits force. The listed leverage ratio is a maker figure, so judge the tool by how it handles a 1/8 inch aluminum rivet. Compared with the long handled NEXTACK, it is quicker for small rivets but less suited to large ones. Compared with the Arrow, it is more compact and has tool free nose changes.

Ownership is about the nosepieces and jaws. Keep the nosepieces together, clean the jaws and avoid forcing oversized rivets. Replace a jaw that no longer grips. Its 9 inch length also fits in a tool pouch, which makes it handy for roadside or boat repairs where a full size riveter would not travel.
products.bestFor: Quick jobs with small rivets where one hand must hold the work.
pros: One handed use frees the other hand for the work
cons: Short handle limits force on larger rivets
Leverage figure is a maker claim

products.name: NEXTACK 1/4 inch rivet gun kit with 350 rivets and long handles
products.description:
The NEXTACK kit is a long handled two hand riveter that accepts rivets up to 1/4 inch and includes five interchangeable nosepieces and 350 rivets in eight lengths. The long rivets are designed for thick sheet and layered panels.

An eight length assortment is useful because a rivet that is too short fails to set and one that is too long bulges. Compared with the Arrow, the NEXTACK offers bigger capacity and more rivets but needs two hands. Compared with a cordless tool, it takes far more effort for 1/4 inch rivets.

Ownership is about technique. Match the rivet length to the material thickness, hold the gun square to the work and use both hands. Clean the jaws and keep the nosepieces sorted. Because the handles are long, it needs about a hand span of clearance on each side, so check access before choosing it for work inside a panel or a wheel arch.
products.bestFor: Thick metal and large rivets where a cordless tool is not justified.
pros: Eight rivet lengths suit thick material
cons: Two handed operation is slow and tiring
Large kit adds bulk to carry

products.name: Wicks Aircraft 3X pneumatic rivet gun kit with rivet sets and bucking bars
products.description:
This is not a blind rivet tool. The Wicks 3X is a pneumatic hammer gun that drives solid rivets against a bucking bar, the method used in aircraft and vintage metal work. The kit includes the gun, a pressure regulator, a quick connect, five straight rivet sets, two bucking bars and retainer springs.

Solid riveting is a two person or two handed craft, and it takes practice to produce a clean shop head without damaging the skin. Compared with the pop rivet tools above, it demands an air compressor and technique, but it produces joints that a blind rivet cannot match in some applications. It sits at the highest cost tier in the lineup.

Ownership requires a compressor and regulated air. Practice on scrap, set the regulator low and use the correct rivet set for the rivet. Keep the gun lightly oiled and store the sets together. Expect to spend an hour practicing on scrap 2024 style aluminum sheet before touching a real panel, since a poorly formed shop head cannot be fixed without drilling the rivet out.
products.bestFor: Restoration and aircraft style projects that use solid rivets.
pros: Drives solid rivets with a bucking bar
Kit includes rivet sets and bucking bars
cons: Needs a compressor and practice to use well
Not a tool for blind pop rivets

buyingCriteria.explanation: Hand riveters are cheap and need no power, cordless tools are fast and easy on the hands, and pneumatic guns drive solid rivets. Choose by the volume and type of rivets you set. Buyers who set many rivets by hand regret it. The DEWALT and Milwaukee are cordless, the Marson, Arrow, BILITOOLS and NEXTACK are manual and the Wicks is pneumatic.

Rivet diameter sets the nosepiece and force needed. Common sizes are 3/32, 1/8, 5/32, 3/16 and 1/4 inch. Most hand tools stop at 3/16, and 1/4 inch needs long handles or power. The NEXTACK reaches 1/4 inch and the DEWALT reaches 3/16. A quick rule is that the nosepiece, rivet and drilled hole should all match the same nominal diameter, with the hole slightly larger than the rivet body so it can enter freely.

Aluminum rivets need little force, while steel and stainless rivets need far more. Cordless tools list pull force in pounds, a maker figure that depends on the rivet. Manual tools struggle with steel above 1/8 inch. The DEWALT lists up to 2,100 pounds.
Each rivet size needs its own nosepiece. Tool free changes and onboard storage save time. Lost nosepieces are the most common nuisance. The DEWALT and BILITOOLS offer tool free changes.
Extended noses reach tight spots, and long handles give leverage. One handed tools free a hand but have less force. Pick a tool that suits your usual workspace. The Arrow has an extended nose.
The rivet length must match the material thickness. Too short fails to set, and too long bulges. Keep assorted lengths on hand. The NEXTACK kit includes eight lengths.

specDecoder.meaning: Pounds of force the tool can apply to the mandrel. Higher numbers set bigger or harder rivets.
specDecoder.watchFor: The DEWALT lists up to 2,100 lbf, a maker figure.

specDecoder.meaning: A maker estimate of how many rivets a battery will set. It varies with rivet size and material.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Milwaukee lists 450 steel 1/8 inch rivets per charge.

specDecoder.meaning: How much a manual tool multiplies hand force. Higher ratios reduce effort but may need more handle travel.
specDecoder.watchFor: The BILITOOLS lists 27 to 1, a maker figure.

specDecoder.meaning: An interchangeable tip sized to the rivet mandrel. The wrong one jams or slips.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Arrow includes four, and the NEXTACK five.

specDecoder.meaning: A heavy bar held against a solid rivet while the gun hammers the other side.

howWeEvaluated.title: Spec sheet review
howWeEvaluated.description: We evaluated tool type, rivet range, stated force, nosepieces and kit contents from each listing. We compared them with the rivets most users set. The DEWALT and Marson anchored the comparison.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for repeating comments on jammed mandrels, worn jaws, weak springs and wrist fatigue. These issues decide whether a riveter is a pleasure or a chore. Jaw wear and jams came up most.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit for the work
howWeEvaluated.description: Gutters, auto panels, thick sheet and aircraft style work need different tools. We graded each product on those jobs, from the Arrow for light use to the Wicks for solid rivets.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cost relative to the lineup
howWeEvaluated.description: We used relative cost tiers and quote no listing prices. The Arrow and BILITOOLS sit at the low end, while the DEWALT and Wicks sit at the top.

howWeEvaluated.title: Claims we discounted
howWeEvaluated.description: Phrases like professional and heavy duty appear on most listings. We treat them as marketing and rank on stated capacity and build.

cards.label: Cordless
cards.text: The DEWALT and Milwaukee set rivets quickly and spare your hands. They sell as bare tools, so you need a battery.

cards.label: Manual
cards.text: The Marson, Arrow, BILITOOLS and NEXTACK cost less and need no power. They tire your hand on large jobs.

howToChoose.note: Choose cordless if you set more than a few dozen rivets a month, and manual for occasional repairs.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A tool that covers 3/32 to 3/16 inch, with nosepieces stored on the tool and rivets matched to the metal thickness. Drill holes slightly larger than the rivet body.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The DEWALT is the first choice for volume, with the Arrow as the value alternative.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You set rivets weekly or work with steel. A cordless DEWALT or Milwaukee saves time and wear.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You set a handful a year. The Arrow or BILITOOLS is enough.

maintenance.why: Broken mandrels pile up and can jam the tool. Emptying it keeps jaws clear.
Aluminum shavings and mandrel chips cut grip. A brush and compressed air clear them.
Lost nosepieces stop a job. A small case keeps them handy.
Dry pivots stiffen and wear. A drop of oil keeps a manual tool smooth.
Lithium packs last longer at partial charge. Avoid heat and full discharge.

faq.q: What size rivet do I need?
faq.a: Match the rivet to the hole and the material thickness. Common diameters are 3/32 to 1/4 inch, and the length must suit the grip range.

faq.q: Can a hand riveter set steel rivets?
faq.a: Small steel rivets, yes, but it takes strong hands. Above 1/8 inch, a cordless tool is much easier.

faq.q: Are cordless rivet tools worth it?
faq.a: If you set many rivets, yes. They are faster and spare your hands, though they cost far more than manual tools.

faq.q: What is the difference between pop and solid rivets?
faq.a: Pop rivets are set from one side by pulling a mandrel. Solid rivets need a hammer gun and a bucking bar on the other side.

faq.q: Why does my rivet not set?
faq.a: The rivet may be too short, the hole too large or the nosepiece wrong. Check the grip range and the nosepiece.

faq.q: How do I clear a jammed mandrel?
faq.a: Remove the nosepiece and clear broken mandrels from the jaws and the catcher. Keep the jaws clean to prevent a repeat.
